findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById may fail for federated recovery code credentials
findings.body: When `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` returns a credential from federated storage (via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`), the code at line 86 calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. This method is designed for locally stored credentials. If the credential originated from a federated/user storage provider, the ID may not be recognized by the local credential store, causing the removal to silently fail or throw an exception. As a result, exhausted recovery codes from federated storage would never be cleaned up, and the user might not be prompted to generate new ones.

findings.title: NoSuchElementException when credential Optional is empty
findings.body: At line 19, `credentialModelOpt.get()` is called without checking `isPresent()`. If the user has no recovery code credential in either federated or local storage (e.g., credential was removed between page render and bean construction, or a race condition), this will throw `NoSuchElementException` and result in an unhandled 500 error during login. The refactoring to use `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` was an opportunity to add a guard but did not.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are passed to external user storage
findings.body: The `createRecoveryCodesCredential` method serializes the plaintext `generatedCodes` list into JSON and passes it to the external user storage via `UserCredentialModel`. Unlike the local storage path (which hashes codes via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`), the federated path transmits and expects storage of unhashed codes. If the external storage does not independently hash them (as the test implementation demonstrates), recovery codes are stored in plaintext, meaning a compromise of the external store exposes all recovery codes. Consider documenting this security expectation or hashing before transmission.

findings.title: Recovery code validation uses plaintext comparison without constant-time comparison
findings.body: At line 340, `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` performs a plaintext string comparison of recovery codes. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that could allow an attacker to determine valid codes character by character. Additionally, the codes are stored and compared in plaintext (never hashed), unlike the local Keycloak storage path which uses SHA-512 hashing.

findings.title: Raw type List used in JSON deserialization may cause ClassCastException
findings.body: At line 238, `JsonSerialization.readValue(myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData(), List.class)` uses a raw `List` type. The deserialized elements will be `Object` (likely `String` at runtime, but not guaranteed by the compiler). If the JSON contains non-string elements or the deserialization produces unexpected types, a `ClassCastException` could occur at runtime when the list is passed to `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues` which expects `List<String>`. A `TypeReference<List<String>>` should be used instead.

findings.title: getCredential may return stale federated credential when local credential also exists
findings.body: The `getCredential` method prioritizes `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` over `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream()`. If a user has recovery codes in both federated storage and local storage (e.g., after a storage migration or misconfiguration), the federated credential is always returned even if the local one is more recent. This could lead to using outdated or already-consumed codes from the federated storage while ignoring valid local codes.
